title: What the World’s Most Powerful Women Do Differently
summary: The sisters present five research-backed habits of top-performing women, each sourced from a book, study or business school lesson and paired with a case study and a mini exercise. The habits are separating fact from feeling (CBT), ruthless calendar alignment (Essentialism), owning the room with language, asking for feedback before you're ready (Radical Candor), and identity-based habits with 'I am' statements (Atomic Habits).

ideas.idea: Separate fact from feeling: resilience comes from creating space between stimulus and response, not from having no emotions.
ideas.detail: Drawn from cognitive behavioral therapy and Susan David's HBR article 'Emotional Agility'; HBS leadership classes teach emotional regulation alongside leadership and professors say 'separate signal from noise'.

ideas.idea: Use the prompt 'The story I'm telling myself is...' to separate perception from reality and impact from intent.
ideas.detail: A Brené Brown tool the sisters also learned in Stanford's Interpersonal Dynamics (Touchy Feely) class, where the core lesson is separating intent from impact; writing the story down keeps you talking only about impact.

ideas.idea: In tense meetings, write down inflammatory remarks verbatim to reflect on later rather than reacting in the moment, so emotion doesn't distort the data.
ideas.detail: Case study: former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi. Exercise: tonight, jot a triggering moment in two columns, exactly what was said/done versus how you felt, and ask whether the event or your interpretation caused the emotion.

ideas.idea: Success comes from doing less, but better; your calendar must reflect your priorities or someone else controls your time.
ideas.detail: From Greg McKeown's 'Essentialism' (Stanford lecturer who trains execs at Apple and Google). The sisters send calendar invites for everything; if the gym isn't blocked on your calendar, you don't really value it.

ideas.idea: Blocking a non-negotiable on your calendar is a power move and a way to define culture as a leader.
ideas.detail: HBS case 'Sheryl Sandberg: Defining Leadership': she blocked family dinner daily at Facebook, showing priorities by what she did rather than what she said.

ideas.idea: Audit last week's calendar by color-coding green (aligned with values) and red (not), then cut or delegate the red.
ideas.detail: Saying yes to every panel, dinner and meeting lets others subconsciously fill your calendar with obligations you feel you must honor.

ideas.idea: Language doesn't just reflect power, it creates it; the powerful person in a room speaks most clearly, not loudest.
ideas.detail: Taught by Stanford GSB professor Deb Gruenfeld; hedges like 'I just wanted to say' or 'I think maybe' weaken the message and read as uncertainty rather than niceness. HBR's 'Your Words Matter, Talk Like a Leader' covers the gendered dimension.

ideas.idea: Record yourself, count your hedges and filler words ('just', 'sorry', 'I think', 'like'), and rewrite them; replace fillers with a deliberate pause.
ideas.detail: Practice from Jean's Stanford executive communications class. Michelle Obama, in 'Becoming', rehearsed speeches for weeks to strip fillers and studied cadence and pauses like a performer. 'I just wanted to follow up' becomes 'Following up on our last note'. Tools like Read AI now count filler words for you.

ideas.idea: Ask for feedback before you think you're ready; shipping early and often separates fast-growth leaders from those who plateau.
ideas.detail: From Kim Scott's 'Radical Candor', which Jean's LinkedIn manager Albert gave her early in her career. Feedback is a gift, not a weakness.

ideas.idea: People grow from insights, not from praise or critique, and feedback only needs to be directional and timely, not perfect, to be useful.
ideas.detail: The HBR 'feedback fallacy' concept; as a leader, normalize feedback as a habit rather than a performance critique.

ideas.idea: Speak before your thought is perfect: HBS makes class participation 50% of the grade and rewards saying anything at all, a muscle women especially need.
ideas.detail: Cherie describes crafting the perfect smart-sounding comment in her head while the meeting moves on and the moment passes; Jean held herself to a groundbreaking-comment bar that men don't hold themselves to at all. The lesson: believe your contribution is worthwhile.

ideas.idea: Don't set goals, set your identity: say 'I am a writer' rather than 'I want to write', because identity drives action.
ideas.detail: From James Clear's 'Atomic Habits'. Cases: Beyoncé's Sasha Fierce persona as mental priming for performances and interviews; Simone Biles' affirmations ('I am powerful, I am unshakable, I am the best gymnast in the world') as identity locking via neuro-linguistic programming.

ideas.idea: The language around you shapes your identity, so protect it: a partner who calls you a dummy daily chips away at you even if you know you're smart.
ideas.detail: Cherie argues perception is largely what you say and hear; pairing a clear identity with matching language builds the best habits.

ideas.idea: Every morning say your 'I am' statement out loud (I am a CEO, I am calm, I am unshakable) and take one action that reflects it.
ideas.detail: Cherie plays Davina Ho's morning mantra tracks on Spotify and repeats after them for 15-20 minutes, sometimes on the drive to the gym; the sisters ask listeners to share their identities in the comments.
